name: Travancore
info: A princely state at the southern tip of India, built from Venad by Marthanda Varma, which defeated the Dutch at Colachel in 1741, became a British subsidiary ally and merged into independent India in 1949.

facts.founder: Anizham Tirunal Marthanda Varma (r. 1729–1758), who built the small feudal state of Venad into Travancore
facts.predecessor: The kingdom of Venad (Thrippappur Swaroopam), heir of the Ay dynasty and of the Chera kings of Kollam
facts.successor: The state of Travancore–Cochin (1 July 1949), then Kerala (1956) and the Kanyakumari district of Tamil Nadu

t: Travancore's victory over the Dutch East India Company at the Battle of Colachel in 1741 is considered the earliest example of an organised Asian power overcoming European military technology and tactics.
On 3 January 1750 Marthanda Varma dedicated the kingdom to the deity Padmanabha, and its rulers thereafter governed as Padmanabha-dasar, servants of Padmanabha.
Treaties of 1788, 1795 and 1805 placed Travancore under British dominance; after Velu Thampi's rebellion of 1809 almost all its forces were disbanded and the East India Company undertook its defence.
dyk: Chithira Thirunal's Temple Entry Proclamation of 12 November 1936 opened every Hindu temple in Travancore to the backward communities and won praise from Mahatma Gandhi; Swami Vivekananda had earlier called the state "The Lunatic Asylum in India" for its caste discrimination.
ev: Marthanda Varma becomes king of Venad and begins to unify the small kingdoms of the south by brutal methods.
Travancore defeats the Dutch East India Company at the Battle of Colachel and captures Eustachius De Lannoy, who later modernises its army.
On 3 January Marthanda Varma dedicates Travancore to Padmanabha; the kings rule thereafter as servants of the deity.
Travancore defeats the Zamorin of Kozhikode at the battle of Purakkad and becomes the dominant state of Kerala.
On 28 December Tipu Sultan of Mysore attacks the Nedunkotta lines from the north and is defeated at the Battle of Nedumkotta.
Velu Thampi Dalawa's war on the East India Company is crushed; he kills himself to avoid capture and Travancore's forces are disbanded.
On 12 November Chithira Thirunal's Temple Entry Proclamation opens the temples of Travancore to the backward communities.
On 1 July Travancore, which acceded to the Indian Union on 12 August 1947, merges with Cochin to form the state of Travancore–Cochin.

sections.foundation:
Travancore takes its name from Thiruvithamcode, in the present Kanyakumari district of Tamil Nadu, contracted to Thiruvankode and anglicised by the English. The land at the tip of the subcontinent had belonged to the Ay dynasty, the earliest rulers of southern Kerala, whose capital lay first at Aykudi and from the late 8th century at Kollam, where the Persian merchant Sulaiman al-Tajir found an extensive trade with China in the 9th century. As the Ays declined, Venad became the southernmost principality of the Second Chera Kingdom; a Chola invasion destroyed Kollam in 1096, and when the Chera capital Mahodayapuram fell too, the last Chera king Rama Varma Kulasekara moved his seat to Kollam and was probably the founder of the Venad royal house, whose rulers kept the title Kulasekara. In the later 12th century the Thrippappur and Chirava branches of the Ay line merged into the Venad family.

The Chera empire had dissolved by about 1100 and the region split into many small kingdoms until Marthanda Varma, king of Venad from 1729, unified them by brutal methods; in his reign Thiruvithamkoor became the official name. He defeated a union of feudal lords, established internal peace and in 29 years of campaigns extended Venad from Kanyakumari to the borders of Kochi, with his prime minister Ramayyan Dalawa (1737–1756) at his side. The capital had moved in 1601 from Thiruvithamcode to Padmanabhapuram near Kalkulam, where it remained until 1795.
sections.socioeconomy:
Travancore lay in three climatic belts: the rugged, cool eastern highlands, the rolling central midlands and the coastal lowlands of the west. By the 1941 census the state had 6,070,018 people. Unlike the rest of India it divided the rupee into its own units: Cash and Chuckram coins were struck in copper, Fanam and Rupee coins in silver. The rulers spent only a small part of the revenue on themselves, but a famine in 1943 cost about 90,000 lives.

Caste was enforced more rigorously in Travancore than in much of India until the mid-1800s, the government turning the caste order into a religious institution; Nairs and Tamil Brahmins alone dominated the bureaucracy into the early 20th century, and women of the backward castes were forbidden to wear an upper cloth, the cause of the 19th-century Upper Cloth Revolt. Swami Vivekananda called the state "The Lunatic Asylum in India" for its discrimination, and the Vaikom Satyagraha exposed it. The Ayyavazhi sect of Ayya Vaikundar, whom Swathi Thirunal imprisoned and then freed, worked as a reform movement among the downtrodden, and the reform movements of the late 19th century gave Travancore the highest male literacy rate in India. Among the forward castes women held relatively high status, daughters inheriting property and holding the right to divorce and remarry, until laws of the regent Sethu Lakshmi Bayi in 1925 established patriarchy.
sections.military:
The making of Travancore was military. In the Travancore–Dutch War Marthanda Varma's forces defeated the Dutch East India Company, allied to the small kingdoms he was absorbing, at the Battle of Colachel in 1741, a victory counted the first in which an organised Asian power overcame European military technology and tactics. The captured Dutch captain Eustachius De Lannoy defected, became captain of the royal bodyguard and later Senior Admiral, and modernised the army with firearms and artillery. At Purakkad in 1755 he defeated the Zamorin of Kozhikode, making Travancore the dominant state of Kerala.

Under Dharma Raja, who refused to surrender Hindu refugees from Mysore's occupation of Malabar, Tipu Sultan's army entered Cochin from Coimbatore in November 1789 and on 28 December attacked the Nedunkotta and was defeated at the Battle of Nedumkotta. Travancore often fought beside the English East India Company, but the alliance ended its own army. After a mutiny of 1805 against the dalawa Velu Thampi most of the Nair battalions were disbanded, and when Velu Thampi and Paliath Achan of Cochin declared war on the Company in 1809, Company troops beat Paliath Achan at Cochin on 27 February and Velu Thampi's men near Nagercoil and Kollam; the Maharajah sided with the British, Velu Thampi took to guerrilla war and killed himself to avoid capture, and almost all remaining forces were disbanded, the Company undertaking the state's defence.
sections.governance:
The king ruled through a Dewan, assisted by the Neetezhutthu Pillay (secretary), the Rayasom Pillay (under-secretary), Rayasoms (clerks) and Kanakku Pillamars (accountants); districts were run by Sarvadhikaris, and the Valia Sarvahi dealt with neighbouring states and Europeans and signed treaties. In 1856 the state was divided into three divisions, Northern Travancore (Cottayam), Quilon and Southern Travancore (Padmanabhapuram), each under a Divan Peishkar ranking with a British District Collector; by 1911 there were five, Padmanabhapuram and Devikulam largely Tamil-speaking, the rest Malayalam-speaking. Queens and regents ruled in their turn, Gowri Lakshmi Bayi, Gowri Parvati Bayi and Sethu Lakshmi Bayi.

Religion and kingship were bound together. On 3 January 1750 Marthanda Varma dedicated the state to Padmanabha, and the kings ruled as his servants; they were conditionally promoted to Kshatriya status through sixteen mahādānams, until in 1848 Lord Dalhousie warned Uttram Tirunal that Madras would take over the administration if the costly practice did not end. From 1788 Travancore accepted British dominance by treaty, entering a subsidiary alliance in 1795 and losing its political independence under the revised treaty of 1805. The dalawas and dewans grew powerful from Velu Thampi (1799–1809), and after 1811 British officers such as Colonel John Munro held the office.
sections.impact:
Travancore was the most powerful state of Kerala from the 1750s, and its rulers, who spent only a small portion of the revenue on themselves, were unusually popular with their subjects. Dharma Raja's reign (1758–1798), assisted by the Diwan Raja Kesavadas, is counted a golden age of social development, and the reform movements of the 19th century made the kingdom the region with the highest male literacy rate in India. Under Chithira Thirunal the state built heavy industry, twenty public undertakings on local rubber, ceramics and minerals that still form a majority of Kerala's premier industries, launched the first public transport route from Thiruvananthapuram to Mavelikkara and the first telecommunication line, appointed Dr G. H. Cousins the first Art Advisor to a government, and patronised musicians, dancers and Vedic scholars.

The Temple Entry Proclamation of 12 November 1936 opened all the Hindu temples of Travancore to the backward communities and drew praise from across India, notably from Mahatma Gandhi. The state's politics also fed the language movements of independent India: Tamils in the southern taluks founded the All Travancore Tamilian Congress at Nagercoil on 16 December 1945, renamed the Travancore Tamil Nadu Congress in 1946, which under A. Nesamony won 14 seats in the first assembly; the Fazal Ali Commission's report of 1955 gave the four southern taluks to Tamil Nadu as Kanyakumari district on 1 November 1956.
sections.decline:
Travancore's independence had been fading since 1788. Balarama Varma, who succeeded in 1798 at sixteen, was the weakest ruler of the dynasty, and the prime ministers took control; Velu Thampi's rebellion of 1809 left the Company responsible for the state's defence and British officers as dewans. The end came with Indian independence. Chithira Thirunal's prime minister, Sir C. P. Ramaswami Iyer, was hated by the communists; a rising at Punnapra-Vayalar in 1946 set up its own government until the Travancore Army and Navy put it down, and in June 1947 Iyer announced that Travancore would remain an independent country rather than join the Indian Union.

An attempt on Iyer's life followed, and he resigned and left for Madras, succeeded by P. G. N. Unnithan. Witnesses and historians hold that the riots did not sway the ruler; after negotiations with V. P. Menon, Chithira Thirunal agreed to accede to the Indian Union on 12 August 1947. On 1 July 1949 the kingdom was forced to merge with Cochin as the short-lived state of Travancore–Kochi, and on 1 November 1956 Kerala came into being under a governor, its southern Tamil taluks going to Madras State. The twenty-sixth amendment of 31 July 1971 stripped the former king of his remaining powers and privy purse. Chithira Thirunal died on 20 July 1991 after 67 years as ruler and titular Maharaja, and the Government of India issued a stamp on 6 November 1991 commemorating his reforms.

summary: Travancore was the princely state built from Venad by Marthanda Varma after 1729, which defeated the Dutch at Colachel, dedicated itself to the deity Padmanabha, passed under British dominance by the treaties of 1788–1805, and in its last decades opened its temples to all castes and built modern industry before merging into India in 1949.

notes: The article's lede says Marthanda Varma inherited Venad in 1723 and its body says he was king of Venad from 1729 (reign 1729–1758); the profile follows 1729, the register's year.
The Travancore–Dutch War is dated 1739–46 in the lede and 1739–1753 in the body; the military section says so.
The article names the Mysore conflict both as Tipu Sultan's attack of 1789 (Battle of Nedumkotta) and as 'the Travancore–Mysore War (1791)'; the profile uses the dated 1789 battle.

Chithira Thirunal is listed as ruler 1924–1949 (with Sethu Lakshmi Bayi regent 1924–1931) and as reigning 1931 to 1949; the profile gives 1931–1949 for his reign and 67 years to his death in 1991 as the article does.

Left out: the Keralolpathi legend of Parashurama, the titular Maharajas after 1991, the detailed list of dalawas and dewans, and the 1950s politics of the Travancore Tamil Nadu Congress beyond the merger of Kanyakumari.
The article's bibliography and further reading are the sources listed; Hatch (1933) is given with its publisher as the article has it.
